newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Crippling Russian power strikes show reform limits.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Crippling Russian power strikes show reform limits.

text.p: Russian utilities may become a growth area of the country's economy, but crippling power strikes in the Far East show the stark limits of their success.

Strikes by power workers demanding back pay have spread through the Far East from the eastern port of Vladivostok to the volcanic Kamchatka peninsula and up to Siberia's frosty Yakutia region. Workers further west may join the action soon.
"If we don't get emergency help from the federal government...then winter is going to freeze the region," one strike leader said earlier this month.
But the power sector is still favoured by foreign investors. Stock prices, led by Moscow utility Mosenergo, rose more than threefold ahead of the June presidential election.

"The electricity sector in Russia...is obviously headed for strong revenue growth and earnings growth on top of that," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell research chief Jim Nail. He expected utility revenues to soar 75 percent in three to five years.

The question is why investors are looking so favourably at a sector with huge debts and a legacy of crippling government restrictions -- including orders banning firms from cutting off key suppliers in industry and the military.

"It is a vicious circle -- utilities are owed billions and billions of dollars by their customers and they owe billions and billions of dollars back to their suppliers, the government, and their employees," said Nail.
Vladimir Konovalov, chief economist at the World Bank in Moscow, said low domestic prices were partly to blame for the crisis.
"Local energy regulators have tried to keep prices down for consumers and have shot themselves in the foot," he said.
Power stations are an obvious example of an acute cash flow problem hitting Russian industry, where firms often barter for supplies and pay workers in kind.
United City Bank energy analyst Natalya Ivanova estimated Russian firms pay only 15-20 percent of their power bills in cash.

She said one Siberian timber plant pays for power in a barter scheme which involved 20 companies, beginning with timber shipments to a paper maker and ending with deliveries of cars and trucks to the timber plant's electricity supplier.
Firms without cash pay workers in with the goods they make -- with refrigerators at a refrigerator factory, for example.
But power plants have nothing to barter.
"A power plant cannot pay wages with its own products, unlike companies which produce consumer goods," said Ivanova.
A 1995 presidential decree -- now expired -- made it illegal for utilities to cut off supplies to important consumers, such as municipalities and the defence sector.
But with workers across Russia owed 36 trillion roubles ($6.7 billion) in back wages at the end of August some firms fear strikes will spread before the economy can right itself.
"We will have a very big problem in Russia," said Oleg Deripaska, chief executive of Russia's third largest aluminium smelter, Sayansk Aluminium. "Strikes will happen more often."

Perched on Siberia's rolling steppe in the middle of the vast country, Deripaska said Sayansk had advanced $1 million in mid-September to the local hydroelectric utility, which other customers had not paid, to end a week-long strike.
"A lot of workers saw they got results -- they made a show and they got money," said a worried Deripaska. Workers at the power station then sent a note of solidarity to strikers in the Far East.
Ivanova said conditions could be ripe for strikes at 10 of Russia's 89 regional utilities, including Samarenergo, located some 900 km (560 miles) southeast of Moscow.

But economists said Russian industry was unlikely to face a country-wide strike, in part because the authorities are ready to allow local power firms more independence and give utilities the possibility of generating profit.
Morgan Grenfell's Nail said utilities would probably shed jobs and increase rates for some household consumers, who pay 10 percent of the average cost of electricity in western Europe.
These measures should improve the wage picture for workers, but would make life even more difficult for ordinary Russians.
"The payment problem is temporary," Nail said. "The power companies will muddle by." He said Mosenergo's collection rate rose to 78 percent recently from about 55 percent last year.
The World Bank's Konovalov said the government was unlikely to cave in to industry and local government subsidy demands.
"In the old days you could force a subsidy from Moscow to get out of such a predicament, but Moscow doesn't have the money any more," he said.
